title: Chapter 9: The First Ring
blurb: Fallowby's protest costs Hobsmere a player before the last match, and Sorrel finds a number in the Loft's old books that nobody was meant to ask about.

blocks.text: The rain came across the levels on Tuesday evening in long grey veils, one behind another, and the lapwings that had been working the wet pasture behind the Dyke Arms gave it up and went down into the rushes. Inside, Wilfred Cobbing laid an envelope on the table between the glasses. Court paper, cream and heavy. A protest from Fallowby Wardens: Hobsmere's Reed, Lucas Mbeki, was an undeclared sighted player. It was signed in a precise, unhurried hand: Clemency Stannard.

The protest quoted the rule word for word, the way she quoted everything. Sighted players may play but must declare their sight at the Ringing; an undeclared sighted player who is found out is suspended for one match. Under the letter lay the Tuesday Courier, open at the page with Rhys on it, his left side, and under the photograph the line he had told me about on the bus, printed now for the whole Circuit: Dorne to Fallowby Wardens next season.
Everyone at the table turned to look at Rhys.

He put both hands flat on the wood. "No," he said. "Joan. Abel. Mercy, look at me. I didn't know. How does a man tell what he doesn't know? I swear it on my hair, and you all know what my hair costs me." Nobody laughed, and he heard that nobody laughed, and the joke went out of his face. He turned down the table. "Clocks. Is it even true?"
Lucas had gone the colour of the rain on the window. He set his glass down very carefully, as if there were a mechanism in it that might slip a tooth.
"It is true," he said. "I w-was always going to say. I kept finding a reason to wait."
Mercy put her hand over her mouth. Abel looked at the fire. Joan looked at nothing, and I knew she was keeping the Loft yard shut behind her teeth, as I was.
"Rhys didn't tell her," I said. They all looked at me then. "He told me on the bus he would fly every yard for us on Saturday. I believe him."
Rhys looked at me the way he had in the bus window, as if kindness were the one thing he had no answer ready for, and said nothing at all.

The Court heard it on Wednesday morning at the Ringing House. The rain had gone through in the night and left the sky rinsed thin and pale over Wenlode, and all the way up the hill from the station there were rooks on the ploughed strips behind the houses, black on wet brown, lifting and dropping and lifting again, as if the ground were too cold to keep still on.

Augusta Stannard presided, as she had at the inquiry. The clerk read the first statement aloud. It was sworn by Tarrow Dyke's Wing, who had been on the field on Saturday and had seen Lucas look up at the Loose a breath before my first shades rose, and follow them with his eyes. Then Clemency stood, in grey and gold, and lowered her voice, so that the whole room leaned to hear her.

"At Fallowby in the autumn," she said, "when Hamish Toller was still Hobsmere's Wing, I saw Lucas Mbeki give the same look across the Loose. Once. One look is not proof, and I let it go. With a second witness under oath, the rule's words are plain."
Augusta asked whether Lucas Mbeki wished to answer. He stood up straight as a clock hand.
"I am sighted," he said. "I have been since I w-was nine. I did not declare it at any Ringing, this season or the last, and I should have. Nobody at Hobsmere asked me to keep it."
That was true in its words, and I felt every one of them land on Joan and on me.

"The protest of Fallowby Wardens, received by this Court on Monday, is upheld," Augusta said. "Lucas Mbeki is suspended for the match of Saturday next, Hobsmere Cutters against Fallowby Wardens, at Hobsmere. His registration stands." She did not look at me at all, and I felt that more than if she had.
With Hamish still up among the pines, Hobsmere had five fit players.
Rhys was out of his seat and after Clemency into the corridor before any of us could catch his sleeve.
"Tell them," he said. "Tell my crew I never said a word to you."

She turned. "Rhys Dorne told me nothing. He has not spoken to me since he signed, which I took for manners." Her eyes came to me. "Nor could I have watched you at Tarrow Dyke, Sorrel Tansley. Fallowby flew at home that Saturday, in the same light as you. Every club flies every Saturday."
"Then why send it to you?" Joan said. "Why not Tarrow's own name on it?"

"Because Tarrow's Wing would not put Tarrow's name to a protest that might save Tarrow from the drop," Clemency said. "So she sent it to the club that meets you next." She drew on her gloves, finger by finger. "I said in this building once that I would rather beat you on a Reedbed. It is still true. This is the rule, not the Reedbed." She went away down the corridor without hurrying.

Joan had her coat buttoned to the throat, and from the inside of it she took an envelope. She had carried it up the hill that morning with Wilfred walking beside her as if it held eggs: the club tin, and her own savings on top. She went to the clerk at the die press and set it down.
"One registration for Hobsmere Cutters," she said. "Anyone. Wilfred, if it comes to that."
"I'm sixty-one," said Wilfred, "and I run like a sluice gate. But I'll stand where I'm put."

The clerk did not argue. He came round the desk and walked Joan to the door, and showed her the notice still pinned beside it, dated the Friday of the draw for the sixteenth matchday, noon. Registration for Season CCIII was closed. After the close a club might field only players already registered this season.
Joan read it all the way to the bottom, though she had read it before. She thanked him. She put the envelope back inside her coat.

At the foot of the hill, where Mercy and Abel were waiting by the station railings, she said, "Silt and back-flow," once, and then she told them plainly. "I saw that notice the day it went up at the Loft. I let it pass. The fee was the whole tin, and there's not a soul in Hobsmere who'll stand by that mere for us. That's mine. It isn't Lucas's."

That night at the Dyke Arms the crew wanted someone, the way a field wants a drain after rain. Mercy said that if Lucas had only declared in the autumn they would at least have known where they stood. Abel said, to the fire, that if there had been a sixth name on the list there would be six rings on Saturday. Lucas sat at the end of the table writing to Hamish, a careful letter in a small exact hand, setting each word down like the teeth of a wheel, and did not defend himself once.
"Nobody at this table puts it on Lucas," Joan said. "You want a sump to pour it down, pour it down me. I've silt enough to take it."

She was not looking at Lucas when she said it. She was looking at the black window on the mere side, and her face had the look I had seen once in the Loft yard, something older than anger. I did not know what it was about. I knew it was not about Lucas, and that she would not thank me for asking, and I put my hand on her wrist under the table and left it there.
Lucas folded his letter in three and posted it in the box at the causeway end before he went home.

On Thursday Pollard met us at the far end of the causeway, on his own side, with his watch in his hand and his chalk in his pocket. The wild roost was coming in. From every quarter of the fen the starlings were arriving in long loose strings, low over the drains, drawing in toward his reed, and the strings met and thickened and became one great breathing shape that leaned and folded over the water in the last of the light. It was thinner now than in midwinter. Here and there two birds came in close together and kept apart from the rest, and I knew it was the spring in them.

We held our Ringing on the swept floor of his barn, from the club box, five rings. I closed Joan's, CCIII 23, over the place where the withy sits on match days. Mercy's and Abel's. Then Rhys held out his wrist, and I closed his slowly, my thumb on the stamp, CCIII 26, gently, the way I always close it.
"Still want me on the west edge, Crate?" he said.
"Yes," I said. "Always."
He looked down at the copper and did not narrate anything. Then I closed my own.
"Under ten," Pollard said. "Nine by this, and I call it." There would be no tether tonight and no drift.

I raised my five over the wild birds, and we practised the only thing left to us, how five run round one bird. Rhys went out wide along the bank, saying under his breath that Dorne was away down the west edge and the crowd were on their feet, and Joan told him the crowd was a heron and to shut his gob. The wild birds would hold nothing we showed them past the night. It was our feet learning, not their wings.
Within a minute of my first shade rising, it was there.

It did not keep to the edge. It came in out of the folding mass of the roost, straight and unhurried, and took up its place not at my shade's wingtip, where it had flown through three matches, but against it, closer than any real bird would come, and I felt my shade drawn toward it, gently, the way a current draws a boat that has slipped its mooring. I held my ceiling. It held beside me. It was testing something, and I did not know what.
Pollard had his back to that side of the sky. Without turning, he put his hand into his coat and held out his lens, the strong brass one he reads the feeder rings with, and I took it.

Through my own loft glass I had never been able to read the number. Through his I could. The ring was old copper gone green at the seam, and on one side was the numeral I, for Season I, and on the other, worn almost smooth, a shallow upright groove that could only be one thing.
"It's number one," I said, low, so that only he would hear. "It's wearing number one."
The number the clerk had told me, my first day in the Ringing House, was struck out of every season's issue and kept for the first Wing.
Pollard looked out at the mere for a long time. "The first ring," he said, and let the rest go out over the water with the wind.
"For the first Wing," I said.

"Nine," he said, and I dropped all five, and the wild birds poured down into the reed with a sound like a long breath let out. Joan cut the rings off with the wire snips from the club box, one by one, and dropped the bands into the box for Wilfred to take up to the Loft on the morning train.

On Friday at noon I stood at the public rail of the Circuit Loft and watched the loft-master put his hand into the worn felt bag I had held for him every Friday for three winters. Tenpenny for Hobsmere against Fallowby. Through the wall I could hear the Tenpenny birds already quarrelling over the water in their travelling crate.
When the room had emptied I asked him for one favour, and he looked at me a while and then lifted the flap of the rail.

The ring ledger lives in the back office, where it always smelled of grain and lamp oil and the warm dust that comes off birds, and through that wall the Mallow birds were shifting on their perches, low and sleepy, the way they always are by afternoon. I had swept that floor a hundred times and never opened the books. This season's page was in the boy's round hand. Every ring issued, every ring cut. My own training bands were there, the ones Joan cut after my first training flight, and at the bottom, in ink still bright, the five from last night, entered that morning.
I asked for Season I.

He had to fetch it down from the top shelf, and he blew on it before he gave it to me. The calf was cracked at the spine, and the paper had gone the colour of reed in winter. The rings were entered by number and match, with no names at all. Every ring on the page had its cutting beside it, all down the season, in a slanting brown hand. The last match on the page was the Long Final. Beside it, No. 1: issued for the Long Final. In the cutting column, nothing. Not a line, not a stroke. Just the old paper.

I turned to Season II. The first line read: No. 1, struck by standing order, unissued, for the first Wing. Season III said the same. So did every season after it, two hundred times over, the same words at the head of every page, each in a different hand, the ink going from brown to black as the years came on.
"Nobody's asked for that book in my time," the loft-master said.
I closed it carefully, the way you put a bird back on its perch, and gave it to him with both hands.

Then I walked up the hill to the Ringing House. The clerk was at his die press, and he nodded to me and went on stamping. The charter hung where it had always hung, in its frame by the stair, and I stood under it and read the line in the plainer hand.
The Long Final stands open until the first ring is opened.

The first ring had never been cut. Two hundred seasons of the Loft's own clerks had written down every band that ever went on a wrist and every band that ever came off one, and that one alone had gone on and never come off. It was not lost. It was flying. I had seen it last night against my own shade, and on Saturday at Tarrow, and on the day I first counted to forty-one. And if the first ring had never been opened, then the Long Final, by the charter's own words, still stood open, two hundred years on, on a wall that anyone in Wenlode could walk up the hill and read.

I did not know what that meant. I did not know what a Long Final was, past the name, or what it would ask of anyone. I only stood there in the cold stone light with my heart going like a bird held in the hand. At the end of the corridor was the door of the Clerk's room, and Augusta Stannard walked past this frame every morning of her life.

I caught the 2:10 home, the reed standing gold along the line in the low sun, and thought about tomorrow. At the Ringing I would close five rings, not six, and across the table Fallowby's Wing would close six and know exactly how many I had. The Seven needs seven, and the cure for it was in Clemency Stannard's hands.
